name: Bhutan
tagline: Dzongs, cranes and chilli cheese, valley by valley
meta_description: Plan Bhutan with honest numbers: SDF rules for Indians and international guests, road trips from Siliguri, Paro, Punakha, Phobjikha and Bumthang.
summary: Bhutan is a Himalayan kingdom of about 38,394 sq km where every valley is run from a dzong and every tourist pays a nightly Sustainable Development Fee. Indians pay ₹1,200 a night and can drive in from Siliguri via Phuentsholing; most other visitors pay USD 100 and fly into Paro. Go March–May or late September–November.
intro: Bhutan sits between Tibet and India on the eastern arc of the Himalaya, with a little over 800,000 people spread across 20 districts, each with its own dzong: a monastery and government office under one roof. We plan trips here the way locals move: Paro and Thimphu in the west, over the Dochu La to the old capital Punakha, across the Pele La to the crane valley of Phobjikha, then east to Trongsa and the four valleys of Bumthang.

Two rules shape every Bhutan budget. First, the Sustainable Development Fee (SDF): as we understand it, USD 100 per person per night for most international visitors and ₹1,200 (Nu 1,200) per night for Indian nationals, with children 6–12 paying half and under-6s exempt. Second, Bhutan's Tourism Rules and Regulations 2024 require a licensed guide for tourists beyond the first checkpoint, and the Department of Tourism restated this in April 2026. Check current status before you travel.

For Indian travellers the road is the cheapest door. Indians need no visa: a valid passport or voter ID (EPIC) gets you a free entry permit at Phuentsholing or Paro, or online in advance. A shared jeep from Siliguri to Jaigaon costs a few hundred rupees, and the ngultrum trades at par with the rupee. The real costs are the SDF, the guide and the vehicle, which is why our saver trips share one guide and one vehicle across a small group.

What we love here is how close the old Bhutan sits to the road. Monks still winter in Punakha Dzong at the meeting of the Pho Chhu and Mo Chhu. Black-necked cranes from the Tibetan Plateau land in Phobjikha in late October. Bumthang farms buckwheat and weaves yathra wool. Archery has been the national sport since 1971, and every village has a range. Our pages give you the facts, the fees and the drive times.

story.title: How the dragon kingdom kept its forests

chapters.heading: Temples pinned on a demoness
chapters.text: Bhutanese history usually starts with a legend. In the 7th century the Tibetan emperor Songtsen Gampo is said to have built 108 temples on a single day to pin down a giant demoness lying across the Himalaya. Two of them survive in Bhutan: Kyichu Lhakhang in Paro and Jambay Lhakhang in Bumthang. A century later Padmasambhava, whom Bhutanese call Guru Rinpoche, came to Bumthang to cure the local king Sindhu Raja and left a body print in a cave at Kurjey. He is also remembered at Taktsang, the cliff above Paro where he is said to have arrived on the back of a tigress. Nearly every tshechu festival you can attend today honours him.

chapters.heading: The Zhabdrung and his fortresses
chapters.text: In 1616 a Drukpa lama called Ngawang Namgyal crossed from Tibet into the western valleys. Known as the Zhabdrung, he unified them into one state, beat back Tibetan invasions and built a chain of dzongs: Simtokha in 1629, Punakha in 1637–38, Wangdue Phodrang from 1638, Paro's Rinpung Dzong in 1646 and Trongsa in 1647. Each held monks in one courtyard and administrators in the other, a pattern Bhutan still follows. He also laid down rules of dress and conduct, the roots of today's Driglam Namzha code, and introduced the gho for men. The country's name for itself, Druk Yul, means land of the thunder dragon, after his Drukpa lineage.

chapters.heading: From Trongsa penlop to king
chapters.text: For two centuries power swung between regional governors. The penlops of Trongsa, whose dzong sat on the only east–west trail and could shut its gates to split the country in two, grew strongest. In 1885 Ugyen Wangchuck won a decisive battle at what is now Changlimithang ground in Thimphu, and in 1907 he was crowned the first king at Punakha Dzong. Every king since has served first as Trongsa penlop. The third king moved the capital to Thimphu, made official in 1961, and opened the first roads from India. The fourth king spoke of Gross National Happiness in 1972 and set in motion the move to an elected parliament, completed in 2008.

chapters.heading: Happiness written into law
chapters.text: Gross National Happiness rests on four pillars named by the government: sustainable and equitable socio-economic development, environmental conservation, preservation and promotion of culture, and good governance. They are not slogans. The 2008 Constitution requires that at least 60 percent of Bhutan's land stays under forest for all time, and forest cover today is above 70 percent, which makes the country a net carbon sink. The first king banned tobacco in 1916; the Tobacco Control Act of 2010 banned its sale outright, until Parliament legalised sales again in July 2021. Even the high SDF follows the same idea: fewer visitors, each paying towards schools, hospitals and forests.

highlights.title: The Tiger's Nest hike
highlights.text: Taktsang clings to a cliff at 3,120 m, about 900 m above the Paro valley. The trail takes 4–6 hours return through blue pine and prayer flags, with a cafeteria at the halfway viewpoint. Built in 1692 around a meditation cave, it was restored after a fire in 1998.

highlights.title: Punakha Dzong at the confluence
highlights.text: Built in 1637–38 between the Pho Chhu and Mo Chhu, Punakha Dzong was the seat of government until 1955 and the coronation venue of every king since 1907. In spring jacaranda trees flower mauve along its walls, and the central monk body winters here.

highlights.title: Cranes over Gangtey
highlights.text: Black-necked cranes from the Tibetan Plateau arrive in the Phobjikha valley in the last week of October and, by local belief, circle Gangtey Goenpa three times. The valley keeps its power lines underground for the birds. A crane festival is held in the monastery courtyard every November.

highlights.title: Bumthang's four valleys
highlights.text: Choekhor, Tang, Ura and Chhume make up Bumthang, Bhutan's spiritual heartland. Here you find Jambay Lhakhang from the 7th century, Kurjey with the first three kings' remains, the Burning Lake, buckwheat fields, yathra looms and Bhutan's own brewery in Jakar.

highlights.title: Chele La and the Haa valley
highlights.text: The road from Paro to Haa crosses Chele La at 3,988 m, the highest motorable point in Bhutan, with views to Jomolhari on clear mornings. Haa below is one of the least populated districts, known for its White and Black temples and buckwheat dumplings.

highlights.title: A tshechu in a dzong courtyard
highlights.text: Each district holds a tshechu, a festival of masked cham dances honouring Guru Rinpoche. Paro's in spring ends with a giant thongdrel unrolled before dawn; Thimphu's runs in autumn at Tashichho Dzong. Locals dress in their best gho and kira and pack lunch.

money_savers: Indian nationals pay ₹1,200 a night SDF against USD 100 for most other passports, so an Indian passport or voter ID is the single biggest saving; carry it with at least six months' validity on the passport.
Enter by road from Siliguri: a shared jeep or bus to Jaigaon costs ₹150–400 a seat, against ₹8,000–20,000 for a one-way flight into Paro.
Travel in a group of four to six: the guide fee and vehicle hire, often ₹6,000–10,000 a day together, are the same whether one or six people share them.
Visit in late November–February outside festival dates, when many mid-range hotels in Thimphu and Paro drop their rates and Punakha stays mild.
Eat where drivers and office workers eat: a plate of ema datshi, red rice and dal in a local Thimphu or Paro restaurant runs ₹200–400.
Apply for your entry permit online before you travel so you do not lose half a day at the Phuentsholing immigration office queue; check current status before you travel.
getting_there: By air, Paro International Airport, at 2,235 m and about 6 km from Paro town, is Bhutan's only international airport. Drukair and Bhutan Airlines fly in from cities that have included Delhi, Kolkata, Bagdogra, Guwahati, Kathmandu and Bangkok; flights land in daylight only, and the left-side window seat usually shows the high peaks on the way in. Routes change, so check current status before you travel. By road, most Indian travellers reach Siliguri (New Jalpaiguri station or Bagdogra airport), then take a bus or shared jeep about 160 km and 4–5 hours to Jaigaon, the Indian town across the Bhutan Gate from Phuentsholing. Hasimara railway station is about 17 km from Jaigaon. From Phuentsholing it is about 150 km and 5–6 hours up to Thimphu or Paro.
permits: As we understand the rules: Indian nationals need a valid Indian passport or voter ID (EPIC) and get a free entry permit at Phuentsholing or Paro, or online in advance; Aadhaar is not accepted. They pay an SDF of ₹1,200 per night. Most other nationalities need a visa arranged through a licensed Bhutanese operator and pay USD 100 per night SDF. Children 6–12 pay half; under-6s are exempt. A licensed guide must accompany tourists beyond the first checkpoint, and districts beyond Paro and Thimphu must be on your permit. Check current status before you travel.

months.summary: January is cold, dry and clear, with the sharpest mountain views of the year from Dochu La. Nights in Thimphu and Paro drop below freezing, so hotel heating matters more than usual. Punakha at 1,200 m stays mild and makes a good base. Few tourists come, so dzongs are quiet and some hotels discount. Passes like Pele La can see snow, which may close the road east for a few hours; check current status before you travel.
months.tip: Pack thermal layers and stay in Punakha for warmer nights.

months.summary: February brings Losar, the Bhutanese New Year, and the Punakha Drubchen and Tshechu, when villagers re-enact old battles with Tibetan armies in the dzong courtyard. Skies are mostly clear and cold. Rhododendrons start to flower at lower levels late in the month. Room rates are still low except around Punakha festival dates. Snow can dust Chele La and Pele La; check current status before you travel.
months.tip: Time a Punakha visit for the late-February festival if dates match.

months.summary: March opens the spring season. Peach and pear trees flower in Paro, rhododendrons bloom on the passes, and the Paro Tshechu usually falls in late March or April. Hotels fill quickly around festival dates, so book three to four months ahead. It is a good month for the Tiger's Nest hike and for the Druk Path trek late in the month, though nights at camp still freeze.
months.tip: Book Paro hotels early if your dates touch the tshechu.

months.summary: April is one of the best months: warm days, flowering rhododendrons above 2,500 m, jacaranda beginning at Punakha Dzong and green rice nurseries in the valleys. The Paro Tshechu often runs into early April, and Bumthang's Ura Yakchoe falls in late April or May in some years. Afternoon haze can hide the high peaks. Expect full hotels and higher rates in Paro and Thimphu.
months.tip: Hike Taktsang early in the morning before the haze builds.

months.summary: May stays pleasant, with more rain in the second half as the monsoon approaches. Jacaranda flowers around Punakha Dzong and the valleys turn green as rice is transplanted. Crowds fall from April and some hotels offer shoulder rates. Haa and Bumthang are fresh and quiet. Flights can be delayed by afternoon cloud, so keep a buffer day before an onward connection.
months.tip: Leave a spare day before any international flight out of Paro.

months.summary: June brings the monsoon to the south first, so the Phuentsholing road sees heavy rain and occasional landslides, while Paro and Thimphu get afternoon showers. Bumthang holds the Nimalung and Kurjey tshechus in late June in some years. Prices are low and hotels are quiet. Pack rain gear and leech socks for walks, and build slack into road days; check current status before you travel.
months.tip: Travel the Phuentsholing road in the morning before afternoon rain.

months.summary: July is the heart of the monsoon. Landslides can block the Phuentsholing–Thimphu highway and the Lateral Road for hours, mountain views are rare and trekking is not advised. Rice terraces in Punakha and Paro are at their greenest, and hotel rates are at their lowest. If you go, keep the trip to Paro, Thimphu and Punakha and allow for delays; check current status before you travel.
months.tip: Keep plans to the western valleys and avoid long eastward drives.

months.summary: August is still wet, with cloud on most passes and slow driving on the main highways. Some travellers like the empty dzongs and green fields, and Indian families on school breaks still come by road. Expect leeches on forest trails and slippery steps at Taktsang. Rates stay low. Keep a flexible itinerary and check road conditions each morning; check current status before you travel.
months.tip: Carry a light rain jacket and shoes with grip for Taktsang.

months.summary: Rain eases through September and the rice turns gold in Punakha and Paro. The Thimphu Tshechu falls in September or October; in 2026 it ran 21–23 September, with the Thimphu Drubchen just before. Hotels in the capital fill for festival dates. Late September is a good start to the autumn trekking season, though the first days can still be cloudy.
months.tip: Book Thimphu stays early if your dates overlap the tshechu.

months.summary: October is peak season: clear skies, harvest in the valleys, the best trekking weather and big festivals in Thimphu (in some years), Haa and Bumthang. The first black-necked cranes reach Phobjikha in the last week of the month. Flights and good hotels sell out, so book three to four months ahead. Nights in Bumthang and Phobjikha drop near freezing.
months.tip: Book flights and hotels well ahead for October.

months.summary: November gives crisp, clear days and the best views from Dochu La. Black-necked cranes settle in Phobjikha, and Gangtey Goenpa holds the Black-necked Crane Festival on 11 November in recent years. Trekking is still good early in the month. Crowds thin after mid-November, though Phobjikha's few hotels fill around the festival.
months.tip: Reserve Phobjikha rooms early for the crane festival.

months.summary: December is cold and clear, with cranes in Phobjikha all month and the Druk Wangyel Tshechu at Dochu La on 13 December. Trongsa holds its tshechu in mid-December. Rates fall and dzongs are quiet. Snow can briefly close high passes such as Pele La and Chele La, so check current status before you travel. Punakha is the warmest base.
months.tip: Combine Dochu La on 13 December with a warm night in Punakha.

faqs.q: How much is the SDF for Indians in Bhutan?
faqs.a: As we understand it, Indian nationals pay a Sustainable Development Fee of ₹1,200 (Nu 1,200) per person per night. Children aged 6–12 pay half and under-6s are exempt. You pay it with your entry permit, online or at Phuentsholing or Paro. A 6-night trip for two adults adds ₹14,400 in SDF alone. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the SDF for international tourists?
faqs.a: Most international visitors pay USD 100 per person per night, a reduced rate announced in 2023 that runs to 31 August 2027 as we understand it. It is collected with your visa through a licensed Bhutanese operator. Children 6–12 pay half and under-6s pay nothing. The fee funds health, education and conservation. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Which ID do Indians need to enter Bhutan?
faqs.a: An Indian passport valid for at least six months, or a voter ID card (EPIC). Aadhaar and driving licences are not accepted. Children under 18 without either can usually use a birth certificate with a parent. You get a free entry permit at Phuentsholing or Paro, or online in advance. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide in Bhutan?
faqs.a: Yes, for almost everyone. Bhutan's Tourism Rules and Regulations 2024 require a licensed guide for tourists beyond the first checkpoint, and an April 2026 Department of Tourism notice said guides must accompany guests at all times, including between Paro and other districts. You can stay in Phuentsholing town without one. Treks need a licensed trekking guide. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I travel Bhutan cheaply from India?
faqs.a: Yes, by road. Reach Siliguri, take a shared jeep or bus to Jaigaon for ₹150–400, cross into Phuentsholing and share one guide and vehicle among four to six people. With ₹1,200 SDF, a simple hotel and local meals, budget ₹4,500–6,500 per person per day. Our saver trips start at about ₹22,500 for 4 nights.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Bhutan?
faqs.a: March to May and late September to November. Spring brings rhododendrons and the Paro Tshechu; autumn brings clear skies, harvest, the Thimphu Tshechu and the cranes in Phobjikha from late October. December to February is cold but clear and cheap. July and August are the wettest months, with landslides on the main highways.

faqs.q: Is Bhutan safe for solo women travellers?
faqs.a: Bhutan has a reputation as one of South Asia's calmer countries, and solo women travel here regularly. Because a licensed guide accompanies you, you are rarely alone on the road. Use normal care at night in Phuentsholing and Thimphu bars. If you prefer, ask your operator for a woman guide; several agencies can arrange one.

faqs.q: Do Indian rupees and cards work in Bhutan?
faqs.a: The ngultrum is pegged at par with the rupee, and Indian notes are accepted widely in towns. Carry ₹100–500 notes. ATMs of Bank of Bhutan and Bhutan National Bank exist in Thimphu, Paro and Phuentsholing, but foreign card acceptance is patchy. Some merchants accept Indian UPI QR payments, a link launched in 2021, but coverage is uneven, so carry cash.

faqs.q: Will my phone work in Bhutan?
faqs.a: Indian SIMs roam at high cost and some do not work at all. Buy a local B-Mobile or TashiCell SIM with your passport or permit copy for a few hundred ngultrum plus data packs. Coverage is good in towns and along most of the main highway, and patchy on high passes, in Phobjikha and on treks. Hotel Wi-Fi is common in Thimphu and Paro.
